Defile
de-file'
v. (to make unclean, to pollute; rendering Hebrew tame, Greek koinoo and miaino)
From Old French defouler, to trample, crossed with the Saxon fylan, to make foul. Greek koinoo is instructive: it means to make common, so that to defile a thing is to strip it of its separateness — the opposite of sanctifying.

Biblical Definition

To defile is to make unclean, and our Lord fought his sharpest battle over the direction the defilement travels. The Pharisees held that uncleanness entered from outside, through unwashed hands and forbidden foods. He denied it: “Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man” (Matthew 15:11), and Mark records the conclusion baldly: “That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man” (Mark 7:20). The list that follows — evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, blasphemies — locates the source in the heart, and Mark adds the editorial note that in saying this he was purging all meats. Paul applies the word to the church as a building: “If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” (1 Corinthians 3:17) — a warning aimed at men splitting a congregation into parties. And Hebrews names the mechanism by which one man's bitterness spreads: “lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled” (Hebrews 12:15). A root works underground, appears late, and by the time it is visible it has already fed on a good deal of soil.

Webster 1828 Definition

To make unclean — in Greek, to make common. Christ reverses the assumed direction: defilement comes out of a man, not into him. Paul warns against defiling the church, and Hebrews against the root of bitterness.

expand to see more

DEFILE, v.t. [Sax. fylan, to make foul.] To make unclean; to render foul or dirty; in a general sense.

2. To make impure; to render turbid; as, to defile a stream.

3. To soil or sully; to tarnish; as reputation.

4. To pollute; to make ceremonially unclean, as by the touch of a dead body.

5. To corrupt chastity; to debauch; to violate.

Key Scripture

Mark 7:20 — "And he said, That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man."

Matthew 15:11 — "Not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man; but that which cometh out of the mouth, this defileth a man."

1 Corinthians 3:17 — "If any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are."

Hebrews 12:15 — "Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled;"

Modern Corruption

Defilement is treated as environmental — a matter of what a man is exposed to rather than what proceeds from him — which is precisely the Pharisaic error Christ overturned.

expand to see more

Mark 7 records the argument and it recurs in every generation. The Pharisees had built a fence of external observances on the assumption that holiness is preserved by controlling contact, and our Lord's answer went to the root: nothing entering from outside can defile the heart, because it does not enter the heart. The instinct survives in two forms today. One is a Christian version that measures faithfulness by separation — what is avoided, watched, read, and eaten — and can produce a scrupulous person with an untouched heart. The other is the secular version, which explains wrongdoing entirely by environment and upbringing, and therefore locates the cure in changing conditions. Both agree that the trouble comes from outside. Christ says it comes out. This is not an argument against prudence; a man who knows his own heart will avoid what provokes it. But avoidance is a strategy, not a cleansing, and no arrangement of circumstances has ever changed what proceeds from within.

The principle to recover is that the remedy must therefore be a new heart. If defilement came from outside, better fences would suffice; because it comes from the heart, only regeneration answers it. Ezekiel promises exactly this — a new heart and a new spirit, the stony heart taken away. And Hebrews 12:15 shows the practical shape of the doctrine in a congregation: the church is told to look diligently, because a root of bitterness is not visible at first and defiles many by the time it is. Watching over one another is not intrusion; it is the ordinary means by which God keeps a body clean.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tame is to be or become unclean. Greek koinoo is to make common, the opposite of setting apart; miaino is to stain or pollute.

expand to see more

Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be unclean, to defile; the standard term of the Levitical law.

Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to make common; used of profaning the sabbath and the sanctuary.

Greek koinoo (G2840) — to make common, to defile; the verb of Matthew 15:11 and Mark 7:20.

Greek miaino (G3392) — to stain, to pollute; used of conscience and mind defiled, Titus 1:15.

Greek phtheiro (G5351) — to corrupt, to destroy; the verb behind defile the temple, 1 Corinthians 3:17.

Usage

"Of the direction of defilement: that which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man (Mark 7:20)."

"Of the church as a temple: if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy (1 Corinthians 3:17)."

"Of bitterness spreading: lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you (Hebrews 12:15)."
